stem_md:
Determine all triples  $(x,y,z)$  of positive integers such that
\[\frac{13}{x^2}+\frac{1996}{y^2}=\frac{z}{1997} \]
solution_md:
Expanding, we have

[center] $\frac{13y^{2}+1996x^{2}}{x^{2}y^{2}}=\frac{z}{1997}\Longleftrightarrow 1997\left ( 13y^{2}+1996x^{2} \right )=zx^{2}y^{2}$ [/center]

Note that  $1997\mid zx^{2}y^{2}$ . As  $1997$  is a prime number, then it must divide  $x^2 $ ,  $y^2 $  or  $z$ . Suppose it does not divide  $z$ , then

[center] ${1997\mid x^2 y^2=\left (xy  \right )^2\Rightarrow 1997^2\mid zx^2y^2=1997\left (13y^2+1996x^2  \right )\Rightarrow 1997\mid 13y^2+1996x^2}$ [/center]

This can be written in terms of congruences as

[center] $13y^2+1996x^2\equiv 0\pmod {1997}\Longleftrightarrow 13y^2\equiv x^2\pmod {1997}$ [/center]

So  $13y^2$   is a quadratic residue modulo  $1997$ . But the **Law of Quadratic Reciprocity** gives us an easy contradiction:

[center] ${\left ( \frac{13y^{2}}{1997} \right )=\left ( \frac{13}{1997} \right )\left ( \frac{y^{2}}{1997} \right )=\left ( \frac{13}{1997} \right )=\left ( \frac{1997}{13} \right )=\left ( \frac{8}{13} \right )=\left ( \frac{2}{13} \right )^{3}=\left ( \frac{2}{13} \right )=-1}$ [/center]

Therefore  $1997\mid {z}$ . Let  $z=1997w$  for some natural  $w$ , then

[center] $13y^2+1996x^2=wx^2y^2$ [/center]

Now, it is easily seen that  $x^2\mid 13y^2$  and  $y^2\mid 1996x^2$ . So there exists natural numbers  $k$  and  $h$  such that

[center] $\left\{\begin{matrix}
13y^{2}=kx^{2} 
1996x^{2}=hy^{2}
\end{matrix}\right.$ [/center]

These naturals are not equal to  $1$ , otherwise  $13y^2=x^2$  or  $\left ( 2x \right )^{2}\cdot 499=y^{2}$ . In any case we have an expression of the form  $pm^2=n^2$ , with  $m$  and  $n$  integers and  $p$  prime. This is impossible because

[center] $p\mid n^2\Rightarrow p^2\mid n^2=pm^2\Rightarrow p\mid m^2$ [/center]

And consequently in the left hand side  $p$  has an odd exponent, while in the right hand side it appears with an even exponent, a contradiction.

Finding  $x^2$  on the first expression and replacing it on the second one, we have

[center] $1996\frac{13y^{2}}{k}=hy^{2}\Longleftrightarrow 2^{2}\cdot 499\cdot 13=kh$ [/center]

Therefore  $k\in \left \{ 2,4,13,26,52,499,998,1996,6487,12974 \right \}$ . It can not equal  $2^2\cdot 499\cdot 13$  because it would imply  $h=1$ .

By a similar argument exposed on the case  $pm^2=n^2$  it can be proven that, given two prime numbers  $p$  and  $q$ , there are no two integers  $m$  and  $n$  such that  $pm^2=qn^2$ . As we have  $13y^2=kx^2$ , we can put away  $k=2$  and  $k=499$ . We have eight cases to analyze:

<u>Case 1:</u>  $k=4$ Then  $13y^2=4x^2$  whence  $13\mid x$  and  $y^{2}=\frac{4}{13}x^{2}$ , so if we replace that on  $13y^2+1996x^2=wx^2y^2$  we have

[center] $13\frac{4}{13}x^2+1996x^2=wx^2\frac{4}{13}x^2\Longleftrightarrow 13\cdot 2^{2}\cdot 5^{3}=wx^{2}$ [/center]

As  $13$  does not divide any perfect square that divides  $13\cdot 2^{2}\cdot 5^{3}$ , there is no solution in this case.

<u>Case 2:</u>  $k=13$ Then  $y^2=x^2$ , whence  $x=y$ , so

[center] $13x^2+1996x^2=wx^2x^2\Longleftrightarrow 2009=wx^2$ [/center]

The only perfect squares that divide  $2009$  are  $49$  and  $1$ . Let us take  $49$ . Then  $x=7$  and  $w=41$ , consequently  $z=1997\cdot 41=81877$  and we found the solution  $\left (7,7,81877  \right )$ .

Let us take now  $x=1$ , then  $w=2009$  and we found the solution  $\left (1,1,4011973  \right )$ .

<u>Case 3:</u>  $k=26$ Then  $13y^2=26x^2\Longleftrightarrow y^2=2x^2$ , a contradiction since it is  $pm^2=n^2$ .

<u>Case 4:</u>  $k=52$ Then  $13y^2=52x^2\Longleftrightarrow y^2=4x^2$ , whence  $y=2x$ . Replacing it on  $13y^2+1996x^2=wx^2y^2$  we have

[center] $13\cdot 4x^2+1996x^2=wx^2\cdot 4x^2\Longleftrightarrow 512=wx^2$ [/center]

So  $x^2\in \left \{ 1,4,16,64,256 \right \}$ , and we found the solutions

[center] $\left (1,2,1022464  \right ),\left (2,4,255616  \right ),\left (4,8,63904  \right ),\left (8,16,15976  \right ),\left (16,32,3994  \right )$ [/center]

<u>Case 5:</u>  $k=998$ Then  $13y^2=998x^2\Longleftrightarrow y^2=\frac{998}{13}x^2$ , whence  $13\mid x$  and replacing it we have

[center] $998x^2+1996x^2=wx^2\frac{998}{13}x^2\Longleftrightarrow 39=wx^{2}$ [/center]

A contradiction since none perfect square divisible by  $13$  divides  $39$ .

<u>Case 6:</u>  $k=1996$ Then  $13y^2=1996x^2\Longleftrightarrow y^2=\frac{1996}{13}x^2$ , whence  $2$ ,  $13$  and  $499$  divide  $x$ . Replacing it we have

[center] $1996x^2+1996x^2=wx^2\frac{1996}{13}x^2\Longleftrightarrow 26=wx^2$ [/center]

This is an evident contradiction.

<u>Case 7:</u>  $k=6487$ Then  $13y^2=6487x^2\Longleftrightarrow y^2=499x^2$ , a contradiction since it is  $pm^2=n^2$ .

<u>Case 8:</u>  $k=12974$ Then  $13y^2=12974x^2\Longleftrightarrow y^2=998x^2$ . Therefore  $499\mid x$  and replacing it we have

[center] $12974x^2+1996x^2=wx^2\cdot 998x^2\Longleftrightarrow 15=wx^2$ [/center]

And we have an evident contradiction again.

<u>Conclusion:</u> The solutions  $\left ( x,y,z \right )$  are

[center] $\left ( 7,7,81877 \right )$  $\left ( 1,1,4011973 \right )$  $\left ( 1,2,1022464 \right )$  $\left ( 2,4,255616 \right )$  $\left ( 4,8,63904 \right )$  $\left ( 8,16,15976 \right )$  $\left ( 16,32,3994 \right )$ [/center]
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Italy Contests/Italy TST/2000 Italy TST/378863.json

stem_md: Find all pairs  $ (p, q)$  of prime numbers such that  $ p$  divides  $ 5^q \plus{} 1$  and  $ q$  divides  $ 5^p \plus{} 1$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>$ 5^{2p}\equiv 1\mod q$  and  $ 5^{2q}\equiv 1\mod p$ Now,  $ ord_{q}(5)|2p$ , so  $ ord_{q}(5)\equal{}1$ ,  $ 2$ ,  $ p$ , or  $ 2p$ . If  $ ord_{q}(5)\equal{}1$  or  $ 2$  then either  $ 5\equiv 1\mod q$  or  $ 5^2\equiv 1\mod q$ . Thus  $ q\equal{}2$  or  $ q\equal{}3$ .

If  $ q\equal{}2$ , then  $ p|5^2\plus{}1\equal{}26$ , so  $ p\equal{}2$  or  $ p\equal{}13$ . We can check that  $ (2,2)$  and  $ (13,2)$  both work.

If  $ q\equal{}3$ , then  $ p|5^3\plus{}1\equal{}126$ , so  $ p\equal{}2$ ,  $ p\equal{}3$ , or  $ p\equal{}7$ . Again, we see that  $ (3,3)$ , and  $ (7,3)$  are all solutions, but  $ (2,3)$  is not.

We now have solutions  $ (2,2),(13,2),(3,3),(7,3)$ . By considering  $ ord_{p}(5)\equal{}1$  or  $ 2$  then we get the reversed solutions  $ (2,13)$  and  $ (3,7)$ .

Now suppose that  $ ord_{q}(5)\equal{}p$  or  $ 2p$  and  $ ord_{p}(5)\equal{}q$  or  $ 2q$ . Then  $ p|q\minus{}1$  and  $ q|p\minus{}1$ . But  $ q>p$  follows from  $ p|q\minus{}1$  and  $ p>q$  follows from  $ q|p\minus{}1$ , a contradiction.

Thus the only solutions are  $ (2,2),(3,3),(13,2),(7,3),(2,13),(3,7)$ .</details>

stem_md: We are given  $2001$  balloons and a positive integer  $k$ . Each balloon has been blown up to a certain size (not necessarily the same for each balloon). In each step it is allowed to choose at most  $k$  balloons and equalize their sizes to their arithmetic mean. Determine the smallest value of  $k$  such that, whatever the initial sizes are, it is possible to make all the balloons have equal size after a finite number of steps.
solution_md:
The answer is 29. In general, if there are  $ n$  balloons, the answer is  $ P(n) \equal{}$  largest prime divisor of  $ n$ .

To show that  $ k \equal{} P(n)$  is sufficient, use induction on  $ n$ . If  $ p \equal{} P(n)$  is the largest prime dividing  $ n$ , let  $ n \equal{} pm$ . Divide the  $ n$  balloons into  $ p$  groups of  $ m$  each, and using the induction hypothesis to equalize each set of  $ m$  balloons by averaging at most  $ P(m) \leq p$  at each step. Number the balloons at each such set  $ 1$  through  $ m$ , and now equalize all the number 1's (there are  $ p$  of them), then all the number 2's, etc. through all the ones numbered  $ p$ . The result has all  $ n$  balloons equal.

Showing that  $ k \equal{} P(n)$  is necessary is a nice opportunity to introduce the useful concept of  $ p$ -integers. For a given prime number  $ p$ , a rational number  $ a/b$  is a  $ p$ -integer is  $ \gcd(a,b) \equal{} 1$  (namely, the fraction is written in lowest terms) and  $ p$  does **not** divide  $ b$ . Thus  $ 5/12$  is a 7-integer, and  $ 3/6$  is a 3-integer since  $ 3/6 \equal{} 1/2$ . An ordinary integer is a  $ p$ -integer for any  $ p$ . 

The important thing about  $ p$ -integers is that they can be added, subtracted and multiplied. Indeed,  $ \frac {a}{b} \plus{} \frac {c}{d} \equal{} \frac {ad \plus{} bc}{bd}$ . This fraction may not be reduced, but regardless, if  $ p$  divides neither  $ b$  nor  $ d$  then it doesn't divide any divisor of  $ bd$  either. The same goes for the product  $ \frac {ac}{bd}$ . 

It follows that if  $ x_1,\ldots,x_k$  are  $ p$ -integers and  $ p$  doesn't divide  $ k$ , then the average  $ \frac {1}{k}(x_1 \plus{} x_2 \plus{} \cdots \plus{} x_k)$  is a  $ p$ -integer. So, if the initial sizes of the balloons are all rational  $ p$ -integers, and if we repeatedly equalize groups of various sizes that are not divisible by  $ p$ , then the balloon sizes remain  $ p$ -integers. 

Now make the following assumptions: there are  $ n$  balloons,  $ p$  divides  $ n$ ,  $ p > k$ , the initial sizes of the balloons are all integers, and the sum  $ M$  of those sizes is not divisible by  $ p$ . This can obviously always be managed. Since  $ p$  doesn't divide any number less than or equal to  $ k$ , the balloons will always have  $ p$ -integral size. But to make them equal we must make each balloon have size  $ M/p$  which is not a  $ p$ -integer since  $ M$  is not divisible by  $ p$ . This contradiction shows that  $ k$  must be at least as large as any prime dividing  $ n$  in order for us to be able to equalize any initial set of balloons.

stem_md: On a soccer tournament with  $n\ge 3$  teams taking part, several matches are played in such a way that among any three teams, some two play a match. $(a)$  If  $n=7$ , find the smallest number of matches that must be played. $(b)$  Find the smallest number of matches in terms of  $n$ .
solution_md: We draw a graph such that any line between vertices A and B we color in blue iff A played with B, and in red iff A didn't play with B. Let  $D,E,F$  be midpoints of  $BC,CA,AB$ , and  $H$  is the orthocenter of  $\triangle ABC$ . Then the feet of perpendiculars from  $H$  to the sides of  $\triangle DEF$  are collinear, so  $H$  lies on the circumcircle of  $\triangle DEF$ . But note that the midpoint of  $AH$ ,  $H_a$ , is the orthocenter of  $\triangle AEF$ , and lies on the circumcircle of  $DEF$ . stem_md:
Prove that for each prime number  $p$  and positive integer  $n$ ,  $p^n$  divides
\[\binom{p^n}{p}-p^{n-1}. \]
solution_md:
A combinatorial way is this:

From the set of first  $p^n$  naturals , we can select  $p$  of them in  ${p^n \choose p}$  ways. But now, we can group such  $p$ -element subsets in equivalence classes in the following way: $\{a_1 , a_2 , a_3 , \cdots , a_p\} \equiv \{b_1 , b_2 , b_3 , \cdots , b_p\}$  if there exists a  $0 \leq t < p^n$  such that  $$ \{(a_1+t) \pmod {p^n}, (a_2+t) \pmod {p^n}  , \cdots , (a_p+t) \pmod {p^n} \} = \{b_1 , b_2 , b_3 , \cdots , b_p\} $$  For example if  $p = 3$  and  $ n = 3$ , then the  $3$ -element subset  $\{1,5,26\}$  is in the same equivalence class as  $\{2,6,27\}$  ,  $\{3,7,1\}$ ,  $\cdots$  ,  $\{27,4,25\}$ .

It is not hard to see that most equivalence classes have  $p^n$  elements; the only equivalence classes that do not have  $p^n$  elements are those whose elements are of the form  $$ \{a , a+p^{n-1} , a+2p^{n-1}, \cdots , a+ (p-1)p^{n-1}\} $$  There are  $p^{n-1}$  such subsets. Thus  $$ p^n \mid {p^n \choose p} - p^{n-1} $$

stem_md: Find all functions  $f:\mathbb{R}^+\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^+$  which satisfy the following conditions: $(\text{i})$   $f(x+f(y))=f(x)f(y)$  for all  $x,y>0;$  $(\text{ii})$  there are at most finitely many  $x$  with  $f(x)=1$ .
solution_md:
Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}^+\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^+$ which satisfy the following conditions: $(\text{i})$ $f(x+f(y))=f(x)f(y)$ for all $x,y>0;$ $(\text{ii})$ there are at most finitely many $x$ with $f(x)=1$ .
Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(x+f(y))=f(x)f(y)$ 1) preliminary results : $f(x)>1$ and $f(x)\ge x$ $\forall x$ ===================================== If $f(u)=1$ , then $P(x,u)$ $\implies$ $f(x+1)=f(x)$ and so $f(x+n)=f(x)$ and so $f(u+n)=1$ $\forall n$ and so contradiction with $(ii)$ . So $f(x)\ne 1$ $\forall x$ If $f(u)x$ and so $f(x)>x^{\frac 1n}$ And, setting $n\to +\infty$ , we get $f(x)\ge 1$ $\forall n$ and so $f(x)>1$ $\forall x$ Q.E.D. 2) no such function exists ================= Let $A=f(\mathbb R)$ $P(f(x),1)$ $\implies$ $f(f(x)+f(1))=f(f(x))f(1)$ $P(f(1),x)$ $\implies$ $f(f(x)+f(1))=f(f(1))f(x)$ And so $f(f(x))=cf(x)$ for some constant $c=\frac{f(f(1))}{f(1)}>1$ So $f(x)=cx$ $\forall x\in A$ $P(x,y)$ shows that $x,y\in A$ $\implies$ $xy\in A$ and so $x\in A$ $\implies$ $x^2\in A$ and so $f(x^2)=cx^2$ $f(x)\in A$ $\implies$ $f(x)>1$ and so $f(x)^2>f(x)$ $P(f(x)^2-f(x),x)$ $\implies$ $f(f(x)^2)=f(f(x)^2-f(x))f(x)$ $f(x)\in A$ $\implies$ $f(x)^2\in A$ $\implies$ $f(f(x)^2)=cf(x)^2$ And so $cf(x)^2=f(f(x)^2-f(x))f(x)$ and so $f(f(x)^2-f(x))=cf(x)>f(x)^2-f(x)$ and so $f(x)1$ and that $f(x)\in A$ $\implies$ $f(x)^2\in A$ So no such function.

solution_md: As  $DE$  meets  $(DBC)$  at  $M$  which is the midpoint of arc  $BC$ , by Fact 5,  $DE$  is the angle bisector of  $\angle BDC$ . stem_md: Find all triples of positive integers  $(a,b,p)$  with  $a,b$  positive integers and  $p$  a prime number such that  $2^a+p^b=19^a$
solution_md: Notice that we can rewrite the equation as $p^b=19^a-2^a$ Moreover $ u_{17}(p^b)= u_{17}(19^a-2^a)\overset{ ext{LTE}}{=} u_{17}(17)+ u_{17}(a)= u_{17}(a)+1\ge1$ thus since $p$ is prime and $ u_{17}(p^b)\ge1$ , $p$ must be equal to $17$ Substituting this result into our original equation we obtain $2^a+17^b=19^a$ **Case 1:** $17 mid a$ $ u_{17}(17^b)=1\Longrightarrow b=1$ plugging this in yields $17=19^a-2^a$ which forces $a=1$ since $19^a-2^a>17, orall a>1$ which clearly satisfies the original equation Thus $(a,b,p)=(1,1,17)$ is one solution to the equation.**Case 2:** $17\mid a\Longleftrightarrow a=17k$ The equation transforms into $2^{17k}+17^b=19^a$ Inspecting $\pmod 4$ yields $2^{17k}+17b\equiv1\pmod 4$ furthermore $19^{17k}\equiv3^k\equiv(-1)^k\pmod 4$ which forces $k$ to be even. Now let $k=2n$ The equation becomes $2^{17\cdot 2n}+17^b=19^{17\cdot 2n}$ Furthermore looking at $\pmod 6$ we obtain $2^{17\cdot 2n}+17^b\equiv131072^{2n}+(-1)^b\equiv 2^{2n}+(-1)^b\equiv3 ext{ or }5\pmod 6$ However notice that $19^{17\cdot 2n}\equiv 1\pmod 6$ which is clearly a contradiction Therefore there exist no solutions when $17\mid a$ In conclusion $ oxed{(a,b,p)=(1,1,17) ext{ is the only solution for }a,b\in\mathbb{Z}^+ ext{ and }p\in\mathbb{P}}$ $ lacksquare$ .

stem_md:
Determine all functions  $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$  that satisfy
\[f(f(x)+y)=2x+f(f(y)-x)\quad\text{for all real}\ x,y. \]
solution_md: Let $P(x,y):=f(f(x)+y)=2x+f(f(y)-x)$ **Claim:** $f$ is surjective *Proof:* $P(f(x),x)$ yields $f(f(f(x))+x)=2x+f(0)$ thus $f$ is surjective $\square$ .**Claim:** $f$ is injective *Proof:* Let $f(a)=f(b)$ , furthermore since $f$ is surjective let $f(c)=a+b$ $P(a,c)$ yields $f(f(a)+c)=2a+f(f(c)-a)=2a+f(a+b-a)=2a+f(b)\Longrightarrow f(f(a)+c)-f(b)=2a$ $P(b,c)$ yields $f(f(b)+c)=2b+f(f(c)-b)=2a+f(a+b-c)=2a+f(a)\Longrightarrow f(f(b)+c)-f(a)=2b$ Thus from the last two results we obtain that $2a=2b\Longrightarrow a=b$ and thus $f$ is also injective $\square$ . $P(0,x)$ yields $f(f(0)+x)=f(f(x))\overset{\text{injectivity}}{\Longrightarrow}f(x)=x+c$ where $c=f(0)$ So to sum up $\boxed{f(x)=x+c, \forall x\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and some constant }c}$ $\blacksquare$ .

stem_md: The incircle of a triangle  $ABC$  touches the sides  $AB,BC,CA$  at points  $D,E,F$  respectively. The line through  $A$  parallel to  $DF$  meets the line through  $C$  parallel to  $EF$  at  $G$ . $(a)$  Prove that the quadrilateral  $AICG$  is cyclic. $(b)$  Prove that the points  $B,I,G$  are collinear.
solution_md:
$(b)$ Prove that the points $B,I,G$ are collinear.
Problem $(b)$ . Solution If $G,I,B$ are collinear points, then angle between $\overline{IG}$ and $\overline{IB}$ must be equal to $180^\circ$ . From the case in $(a)$ from triangle $GAI$ we have: $\angle AIG = \left(90^\circ - \frac{\gamma}{2}\right)$ , because $\frac{\gamma}{2}=\angle AGI$ as angles from the same segment in circle. Similarly, from triangle $AIB$ we have the relation \[\angle AIB=180^\circ - \left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right) = 180^\circ - \left(90^\circ -\frac{\gamma}{2}\right) = 90^\circ + \frac{\gamma}{2}\] Therefore angle between $\overline{IG}$ and $\overline{IB}$ is equal to $\angle AIG+\angle AIB = 180^\circ$ , hence $B,I,G$ are collinear.

stem_md: For  $n$  an odd positive integer, the unit squares of an  $n\times n$  chessboard are coloured alternately black and white, with the four corners coloured black. A *tromino* is an  $L$ -shape formed by three connected unit squares. $(a)$  For which values of  $n$  is it possible to cover all the black squares with non-overlapping trominoes lying entirely on the chessboard? $(b)$  When it is possible, find the minimum number of trominoes needed.
solution_md:
Let  $n=2k-1$ . The black squares consist of  $k^2$  "odd squares" (both coordinates odd) and  $(k-1)^2$  even squares (both coordinates even). No tromino can cover two odd squares, so we need at least  $k^2$  trominoes to cover all black squares. Impossible for  $n=3$  and also not for  $n=5$ , as  $9$  trominoes would occupy  $27$  squares and  $27>25$ , so there would be some overlap.

For  $n=7$ , it is not hard to find a covering. (14 of the 16 trominoes will come in pairs making up  $2\times 3$  rectangles.)

Now by induction, we can construct optimal coverings for  $n=9,11,...$ : Adding to an  $(n-1)^2$  board a hook of width 2 containing  $n$  odd and  $n-1$  even black squares, and those can be covered by  $n$  trominoes as is easily seen.

stem_md: $(a)$  Prove that in a triangle the sum of the distances from the centroid to the sides is not less than three times the inradius, and find the cases  of equality. $(b)$  Determine the points in a triangle that minimize the sum of the distances to the sides.
solution_md:
This has to be well-known, no?

a) Let the centroid be  $G$ . The distance of  $G$  to  $BC$  is one-third of  $h_a$ , the distance from  $A$  to  $BC$ . Hence by defining similarly  $h_b, h_c$  we have to show that  $h_a+h_b+h_c \geq 9r$ , with  $r$  the inradius of  $ABC$ .

Now if  $\Delta$  is the area of  $ABC$  then we have  $ah_a = bh_b = ch_c = 2\Delta$ , so  $(a,b,c),(h_a,h_b,h_c)$  are oppositely sorted. Hence by Rearrangement Inequality,
\[(a+b+c)(h_a+h_b+h_c) \geq 3(ah_a+bh_b+ch_c) = 6\Delta\]\[ \implies h_a+h_b+h_c \geq 3\frac{2\Delta}{a+b+c} = 9r,\]
as desired.

b) Draw  $ABC$  with  $B$  to the left of  $C$ . For a line  $l_a$  parallel to  $BC$  intersecting  $AB,AC$  at  $B',C'$  respectively, and a variable point  $P$  on  $l_a$ , we see that:
1. The distance  $d(P,BC)$  from  $P$  to  $BC$  is constant;
2.  $d(P,AB)$  is linear in  $PB'$ , and  $d(P,AC)$  is linear in  $PC'$ . Hence moving  $P$  to the left of  $B'$  or to the right of  $C'$  increases both distances, and hence the sum of distances from  $P$  to the sides. Thus we only need to consider points in or on the boundary of  $ABC$ .
3. Furthermore, since the sum of distances from  $P$  to the sides is linear on  $B'C'$ , it attains its minimum at either  $B'$  or  $C'$ . Say it attains its minimum at  $B'$ ; then repeating the above argument with  $l_c = AB$ , we see that the sum of distances to the sides takes its minimum at either  $A$  or  $B$ . A similar argument holds if the minimum is attained at  $C'$ .

Thus the minimum sum of distances is  $\min(h_a,h_b,h_c)$ . If  $BC$  is the unique longest side in  $ABC$  then the unique point minimizing the sum of distances to the sides is  $A$ . If  $BC = CA > AB$  then all points on segment  $AB$  minimize the sum. If  $ABC$  is equilateral then all points inside or on the boundary of  $ABC$  minimize the sum.

stem_md:
Suppose that  $f:\{1, 2,\ldots ,1600\}\rightarrow\{1, 2,\ldots ,1600\}$  satisfies  $f(1)=1$  and
\[f^{2005}(x)=x\quad\text{for}\ x=1,2,\ldots ,1600. \] $(a)$  Prove that  $f$  has a fixed point different from  $1$ . $(b)$  Find all  $n>1600$  such that any  $f:\{1,\ldots ,n\}\rightarrow\{1,\ldots ,n\}$  satisfying the above condition has at least two fixed points.
solution_md:
Since  $f^{2005} = \textrm{id}$ , it follows  $f$  is a permutation, hence a product of cycles  $\prod_{k=0}^s \gamma_k$ , of lengths  $\lambda_k$ , where  $\gamma_0 = (1)$ , so  $\lambda_0 = 1$  (because we are given  $1$  is a fixed point).
We must therefore have  $\sum_{k=1}^s \lambda_k = 1599$ , and  $\lambda_k \mid 2500 = 5\cdot 401$  for all  $1\leq k \leq s$ . But then it means  $\lambda_k \in \{1,5,401\}$ . Since  $1599 = 5\cdot 401 - 401 - 5$ , it is impossible to have all  $\lambda_k \neq 1$ , so there is (at least) one more fixed point. For any  $n>1600$  one can express  $n-1$  as a sum with terms just  $5$  and  $401$  (Sylvester problem, or Frobenius, or the dreadfully-named Chicken McNugget theorem), so the answer is NO, no need to have that extra fixed point.

stem_md: Let  $N$  be a positive integer. Alberto and Barbara write numbers on a blackboard taking turns, according to the following rules. Alberto starts writing  $1$ , and thereafter if a player has written  $n$  on a certain move, his adversary is allowed to write  $n+1$  or  $2n$  as long as he/she does not obtain a number greater than  $N$ . The player who writes  $N$  wins. $(a)$  Determine which player has a winning strategy for  $N=2005$ . $(b)$  Determine which player has a winning strategy for  $N=2004$ . $(c)$  Find for how many integers  $N\le 2005$  Barbara has a winning strategy.
solution_md:
@ocha: your proof fails in the case  $N=8$ .

<details><summary>solution</summary>Consider the binary representation of  $N$ .
If there is no  $1$ -bit at an even position, Barbara has a winning strategy:

If  $k$  is the current position, choose the next position as follows:
Let  $e$  be the unique integer s.t.  $N/2^{e+1} < k \leq N/2^e$ .
If  $e$  is even, do the  $+1$ -move.
Otherwise, do the  $*2$ -move.
The positions  $B$  moves to are exactly the even numbers in the union of intervals  $(N/2^{2i+1}, N/2^{2i}]$  (by induction on  $i$ ).
We see that  $B$  wins.

Otherwise, Alberto can win:
Let  $j$  be the smallest  $1$ -bit at an even position.
Let  $e$  be the unique integer s.t.  $N/2^{e+1} < k \leq N/2^e$ .
Now, if  $e$  is even or  $e \geq j$ , do the  $+1$ -move.
Otherwise, do the  $*2$ -move.
The positions  $A$  moves to are the even numbers in the union of intervals  $(N/2^{2i+1}, N/2^{2i}]$  for  $0 \leq 2i < j$ , and the odd numbers in the union of intervals  $(N/2^{i+1}, N/2^i]$  for  $i \geq j$  (induction again).
Hence  $A$  wins.

For part (c), we count the number of integers with all 1-bits in even positions  $\leq 2005$ . So,  $2005_{10} = 01,11,11,01,01,01_{2} \geq 00,10,10,10,10,10_{2}$ , so the number of solutions is  $0,1,1,1,1,1_{2} = 31_{10}$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $S$  be a string of  $99$  characters,  $66$  of which are  $A$  and  $33$  are  $B$ . We call  $S$  *good* if, for each  $n$  such that  $1\le n \le 99$ , the sub-string made from the first  $n$  characters of  $S$  has an odd number of distinct permutations. How many good strings are there? Which strings are good?
solution_md:
Here's my solution although it's rather long.  Your question is very hard I think cmmmrc. I think that a better solution (if there is one) might be required to answer your question.
**Solution:**

We must prove the following Lemma:

*For all  $i\in\{1,2,\dots,2^n-1\}$ , we have that  ${2^n\choose i}$  is even.*

Proof:

By Lucas' Theorem, we have the result immediately:
 ${2^n\choose i}\equiv {1\choose 0}{0\choose i_k}\dots {0\choose 1}\dots {0\choose i_0}\equiv 0$  mod  $2$ .

where  $i=i_k i_{k-1}\cdots i_0$  is the binary representation of  $i$ .

Knowing this, we can begin the problem.

Now, the number of distinct permutations of a substring is simply  ${n\choose b}$ , where  $n$  is the length of the substring and  $b$  is the number of  $B$ 's in these  $n$  letters.

So if a  $B$  is in the first  $64$  letters, then the number of permutations of the substring with length  $64$  is  ${64\choose x}$ , where  $x\in\{1,2,\dots,33\}$ .  But by our Lemma, the number must be even, and thus the first  $64$  letters must all be  $A$ .

Now, there can only be  $2$  more  $A$ 's in the string, so we have three cases.  If the  $65$ th and  $66$ th letters are both  $A$ 's, then the rest must be  $B$ 's.  However, if  $n=68$ , we have  ${68\choose 2}$  permutations, which is even.  So the first  $66$  letters cannot all be  $A$ 's.

Now, if exactly the first  $65$  letters are  $A$ 's, then the  $66$ th is a  $B$  and for  $n=66$  we have  ${66\choose 1}$  permutations, an even number.

Thus the  $65$ th letter must be  $B$ .

Now comes the tedious part.

Now for  $x\le 33,$  let  $x$  be the number of  $B$ 's and assume that  ${64+x\choose x}$  is odd.  Then if we add a  $B$  to the sequence, then we have  ${65+x\choose x+1}$  permutations, which will remain odd since the greatest power of  $2$  dividing  $x+1$  divides  $65+x$  as well (since  $x\le 33$ ).  But if we add an  $A$  to the sequence, we have  ${65+x\choose x}=\frac{65+x}{65}{64+x\choose x}$  which will remain odd iff  $x$  is even.  Therefore, we can only add an  $A$  if  $x$  is even.

Now, consider the case that added an  $A$  when  $x$  is even.

By the same method, we can show if  ${65+x\choose x}$  is odd (as it should be if  $x$  is even), then by adding a  $B$  we have  ${66+x\choose x+1}=\frac{66+x}{1+x}{65+x\choose x}$  is either not an integer or even.  But, if we add an  $A$  after the other  $A$ , we have that  ${66+x\choose x}=\frac{66+x}{66}{65+x\choose x}$  is an odd integer iff  $x$  is divisible by  $4$ .

So the two  $A$ 's must be together, and  $4|x$ .  Hence the two  $A$ 's cannot be the last two of the sequence ( $4$  does not divide  $33$ ).

Now, we must add a  $B$  after the final two  $A$ 's are gone, but if one  $B$  is used, we are still ok, since  ${67+x\choose x+1}=\frac{67+x}{1+x}{66+x\choose x}$  which is still odd for  $x$  divisible by  $4$ .  However, if we add another  $B$  we have that  ${68+x\choose x+2}=\frac{68+x}{x+2}{67+x\choose x+1}$  which cannot be even if  $4|x$  and  ${67+x\choose x+1}$  is odd.

Therefore, the only string that works (and barely fits) is the string with  $64$   $A$ 's,  $32$   $B$ 's, and finally  $AAB$ .

That's actually quite easy to answer: There is one good string, if {a+b choose a} is odd, and there is no good string, if {a+b choose a} is even. The proof can be done by induction: If {a+b choose a} is even, there is no good string, since the entire string allows an even number of permutations. If x={a+b choose a} is odd, then exactly one of y={a+b-1 choose a} and z={a+b-1 choose a-1} is odd (since y+z=x). Either way you get a unique possibility for extending the string to length a+b. End of proof. Another way of looking at it: You move through the odd entries of Pascal's triangle, downwards, step by step.

The circles  $\gamma_1$  and  $\gamma_2$  intersect at the points  $Q$  and  $R$  and internally touch a circle  $\gamma$  at  $A_1$  and  $A_2$  respectively. Let  $P$  be an arbitrary point on  $\gamma$ . Segments  $PA_1$  and  $PA_2$  meet  $\gamma_1$  and  $\gamma_2$  again at  $B_1$  and  $B_2$  respectively.
a) Prove that the tangent to  $\gamma_{1}$  at  $B_{1}$  and the tangent to  $\gamma_{2}$  at  $B_{2}$  are parallel.
b) Prove that  $B_{1}B_{2}$  is the common tangent to  $\gamma_{1}$  and  $\gamma_{2}$  iff  $P$  lies on  $QR$ .
solution_md:
Let the centres of the circles be  $O_1$ ,  $O_2$  and  $O$  respectively. Then:

(a). Connect  $O_1B_1$ ,  $O_2B_2$  and  $PO$ . Then  $O_1B_1 || PO || O_2B_2$ , which means the tangents at  $B_1$  and  $B_2$  are also paralel.

(b). Since P lies on QR, so  $PB_1 \cdot PA_1 = PB_2 \cdot PA_2$ . Thus  $A_1, A_2, B_2, B_1$  lies on the same circle. Therefore  $\angle{PB_2B_1}+\angle{O_2B_2A_2}=\angle{B_1A_1A_2}+\angle{O_2A_2B_2}=$  $=\angle{O_2A_2B_2}+\angle{OA_2A_1}+\angle{OA_1B_1}=\angle{PB_1B_2}+\angle{O_1B_1A_1}$ 

Thus  $\angle{B_1B_2O_2}=\angle{B_2B_1O_1}$ . But by the conclusion of the part (a) we have that those two angles have the sum of  $180^o$ . So there must be  $\angle{B_1B_2O_2}=\angle{B_2B_1O_1}=90^o$ , which yields  $B_1B_2$  is the common tangent of  $\gamma_1$  and  $\gamma_2$ .

Find all functions  $f : \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$  such that for all integers  $m,n$ ,
\[f(m - n + f(n)) = f(m) + f(n).\]
solution_md:
Let  $P(m,n)$  be  $f(m-n+f(n))=f(m)+f(n)$ . $P(2n-f(n),n)\implies f(2n-f(n))=0$ **Case1:** $f\equiv 0$ This satisfies the condition.**Case2:** $\exists \alpha\in \mathbb Z$  s.t.  $f(\alpha)\neq 0$ If  $\exists n_0\in \mathbb Z$  s.t.  $\beta =2n_0-f(n_0)\neq 0$ . $P(m,\beta)\implies f(m-\beta)=f(m)$ .
This implies that  $f$  is periodic.Thus  $f$  is bounded.On the other hand, $P(m,m)\implies f(f(m))=2f(m)$ .Then $f^{k}(\alpha)=2^{k-1}f(\alpha)$ .Hence  $|f|$  is unbounded which is absurd.Thus $\forall n\in \mathbb Z:f(n)=2n$  which satisfies the condition.

Let  $ABC$  be a triangle, let  $H$  be the orthocentre and  $L,M,N$  the midpoints of the sides  $AB, BC, CA$  respectively. Prove that
\[HL^{2} + HM^{2} + HN^{2} < AL^{2} + BM^{2} + CN^{2}\]
if and only if  $ABC$  is acute-angled.
solution_md:
**<u>Lemma.</u>**  $\boxed {\ \mathrm {\ acute}\ \triangle ABC\Longrightarrow 8R^2<a^2+b^2+c^2\le 9R^2\ }\ .$ 

<u>Proof.</u>  $a^2+b^2+c^2-8R^2=4R^2\cdot(\sin ^2A+\sin ^2B+\sin^2C-2)=$  $2R^2[(1-\cos 2A)+(1-\cos 2B)+(1-\cos 2C)-4]=$  $-2R^2(1+\cos 2A+\cos 2B+\cos 2C)=-2R^2[2\cos^2A+2\cos(B+C)\cos(B-C)]=$  $-4R^2[\cos^2A-\cos A\cos (B-C)]=4R^2\cos A[\cos (B+C)+\cos (B-C)]=$  $8R^2\cos A\cos B\cos C>0\ .$  <u>Remark.</u>  $a^2+b^2+c^2=8R^2(1+\cos A\cos B\cos C)\le 9R^2$ 
because it is well-known that in any triangle  $ABC$ ,  $\cos A\cos B\cos C\le \frac 18\ .$ 
**<u>The proof of the proposed problem.</u>** It is well-knownn that  $AH=2R\cos A$  a.s.o. Therefore, $4\cdot HM^2=2\cdot(HB^2+HC^2)-a^2=8R^2(\cos^2B+\cos^2C)-a^2=$  $8R^2(2-\sin^2B+\sin^2C)-a^2=16R^2-2(b^2+c^2)-a^2\ .$  Thus, $4\cdot\sum HM^2=48R^2-5(a^2+b^2+c^2)\ .$  From the above lemma results the relation $\frac 13 (a^2+b^2+c^2)\le 4\cdot\sum HM^2<6(a^2+b^2+c^2)-5(a^2+b^2+c^2)=a^2+b^2+c^2$ , i.e. $\boxed {\ \frac 13 (AL^2+BM^2+CN^2)\le HM^2+HN^2+HL^2<AL^2+BM^2+CN^2\ }\ .$

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer, and let  $A_{n}$  be the the set of all positive integers  $a\le n$  such that  $n|a^{n}+1$ .
a) Find all  $n$  such that  $A_{n}\neq \emptyset$ b) Find all  $n$  such that  $|{A_{n}}|$  is even and non-zero.
c) Is there  $n$  such that  $|{A_{n}}| = 130$ ?
solution_md:
Fun problem.  I don't think my solution is very tricky, maybe there is a shorter way.

For part a, we make the observation that we can always choose  $a = n-1$  for when  $n$  is odd.  The only exception is 1, but that clearly also works.  Now we consider  $n$  being even.  We have two cases.

Assume  $4|n$ :

This means that  $n = 4k$  so that  $4k|a^{4k}+1$   Since we know that  $gcd(a,n) = 1$ , it is clear that  $a^{4k}\equiv 1 \pmod 4$   Thus, we have a contradiction.

So we know that even  $n$  are of the form  $2k$ .  Where  $k$  is an odd integer.  Now notice that  $a^{n}\equiv-1 \pmod n$  with  $n$  being even.  So we have that  $(a^{\frac{n}{2}})^{2}\equiv-1 \pmod n$   Thus we know that  $-1$  is a square in mod  $n$ .  We conclude that the only prime divisors  $p$  of  $k$  must have  $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ .  I claim that that is indeed all we need.  Notice that  $2k \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ , since  $k$  is odd.  Thus if we have that  $a^{2}\equiv-1 \pmod n$ , then  $a^{2k}\equiv-1 \pmod n$ .  So we would have at least those two solutions.  But of course we could find such an  $a$ .  It is guaranteed by exactly the condition that the only prime divisors of  $k$  are congruent to 1 mod 4.  So we are done.  The answer is all odd  $n$  or even  $n$  of the form  $2k$  where the only prime divisors of  $k$  are 1 mod 4.

Now onto part b.  I think the arguement follows fairly naturally after you decide that they asked only whether or not the number of solutions is even, not to actually count the number.  The answer seems to be for all the  $n$  of the second type listed above except 2.  The ones that are even and have at least one  $a$  that work.  It is easy to prove it for those particular  $n$ .  Since  $n$  is even we have  $a^{n}\equiv (-a)^{n}\pmod n$   So each solution must have another corresponding solution.  The only way this could fail is if  $a \equiv-a \pmod n$ .  But since we have that  $gcd(a,n) = 1$  we know this is only possible when  $n=2$  which is indeed the only exception.  Now we consider the odd  $n$ .  We have to count some solutions by using CRT.  We first prime factor  $n$  and then consider one of the prime powers at a time.  Find the number of solutions in each of those mods and multiply.  Clearly, we are done if we find that there are an odd number of solutions in each mod on its own.  Now we consider the equation we are solving  $a^{n}\equiv-1 \pmod{p^{t}}$   Where we have that  $p^{t}|n$  and that  $n$  is odd.  We have also that  $a^{2n}\equiv 1 \pmod{p^{t}}$ .  Thus, we know that  $ord(a)|2n$  but it doesn't divide  $n$ .  In fact that condition is sufficient since in mod  $p^{t}$  where  $p$  is odd,  $\pm 1$  are the only square roots of 1 (that fact follows directly from factoring or from hensel's lemma).  In other words we are looking for all the elements of mod  $p^{t}$  with certain orders and we are counting their parity.  We take advantage of the fact that the multiplicative group of mod  $p^{t}$  has a generator to conclude that the number of elements with order  $x$  is  $\phi(x)$ .  But we know that  $\phi(x)$  is always even except when  $x = 1,2$ .  We since the order of  $a$  divides  $2n$  and not  $n$ , it is clear it is of the form  $2k$  where  $k$  is odd.  Clearly the only odd number of solutions we are going to get is when  $k=1$ .  But that actually works in this case.  So we are done!

To do part c, we need only be a little bit more careful about the arguement we just used for part b.  Based on part b we need only consider even  $n$  that work.  We start counting solutions again.  So we have that the number of solutions to  $a^{n}\equiv-1 \pmod n$  must be 130.  The way to find these solutions is to first consider each prime power divisor separately again and then multiply the number together using CRT.  Remember that in this case  $n$  has exactly one factor of 2.  In mod  $p^{t}$   the number of solutions is exactly the same order trick again. However, in this case, things with order 2 do not work anymore.  In other words, there is an even number of solutions in each prime power mod.  Thus we can actually only have 1 prime power, since 4 does not divide 130.  This simplifies the problem a lot and leaves us with solving the problem of finding the number of solutions to  $a^{2p^{t}}\equiv-1 \pmod{p^{t}}$ .  Doing a little bit of simplifying with euler we get that  $a^{2p^{t-1}}\equiv-1 \pmod{p^{t}}$ .  Or in other words we have  $ord(a)|4p^{t-1}$  but not  $2p^{t-1}$ .  Which is also a sufficient condition again.  Therefore we conclude  $ord(a) = 4, 4p, 4p^{2}, \cdots, 4p^{t-1}$ .  Keep in mind that these are legitimate orders since  $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ .  How many solutions do we have total?  Based on what we concluded earlier it simply: \[\phi(4)+\phi(4p)+\cdots \phi(4p^{t-1}) = 2(1+(p-1)+(p^{2}-p)+\cdots (p^{t-1}-p^{t-2})) = 2p^{t-1}\neq 130\] Yay!

We will ignore  $n=1,2$ , as these are stupid useless numbers that make life challenging. They only work for part (a).

We claim the answer to part (a) is the following:
Let  $\mathcal P_{\geq 3}$  be the set of odd primes, and  $\mathcal P_{1\pmod 4}$  be the set of primes 1 modulo 4. Then,  $n$  has all prime factors in  $\mathcal P_{\geq 3}$  or  $\{2\}\cup\mathcal P_{1\pmod 4}$ .

Note that if  $4\mid n$ , then clearly
\[\{a^n+1\}\subseteq\{a^2+1\}\subseteq\{1,2\pmod 4\}\]
so thus  $4\nmid n$ . Now, if  $n$  is odd, taking  $a=n-1$  gives
\[a^n+1\equiv (-1)^n+1\equiv 0\pmod n\]
Now, if  $n$  is even, suppose  $p\mid n$ . Then,  $a^2+1\equiv 0\pmod p$  has a solution, so  $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ . For the converse, note that  $p=x^2+y^2$  for any  $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ , and thus we can note  $|x+yi|=\sqrt p$ . Thus,
\[p^k=|(x+yi)^k|^2\]
and thus we can write all powers of  $p$  as the sum of two squares. In particular, we can find a solution to  $p\equiv -1\pmod{p^k}$ , so the solution to (a) is indeed as mentioned.

For part b, we note that if  $n$  is even (and greater than 2), then  $a$  and  $n-a$  both work (clearly  $a=n,\frac n2$  fails). If  $n$  is odd, then clearly note that there are actually  $\gcd(n,p-1)$  solutions to  $x^n+1\equiv 0\pmod p$  - let  $g$  be a primitive root modulo  $p$ , and note this implies that the number of solutions is the number of  $1\leq k\leq p-1$  such that
\[nk\equiv 0\pmod{p-1}\]
which has  $\gcd(n,p-1)$  solutions. As  $n$  is odd, this is odd. Now, by Hensel's Lemma, for a prime power  $p^k\mid n$ , the number of solutions to
\[x^n\equiv -1\pmod{p^k}\]
is  $p^{k-1}\gcd(n,p-1)$ , so applying the Chinese Remainder Theorem, we get the desired result.

For part c, the answer is "no". If  $p_1\neq p_2\in\mathcal P_{\geq 3}$  divided  $n$ , by our above discussion, there are  $4\mid p_1^{k_1-1}\gcd(n,p_1-1)p_2^{k_2-1}\gcd(n,p_2-1)$  solutions, a contradiction. Thus,  $n=2p^k$ , impossible.

stem_md:
Find all  $f: R \longrightarrow R$  such that

\[f(xy+f(x))=xf(y)+f(x)\]

for every pair of real numbers  $x,y$ .
solution_md:
Let  $P(x,y)$  be the assertion  $f(xy+f(x))=xf(y)+f(x)$ .

Let  $f(a)=f(b)$  for some  $a,b$  such that  $f(a)\ne0$ . $P(a,b)-P(b,a)\Rightarrow af(a)=bf(a)$ Assume  $f(0)\ne0$ . $P(0,0)\Rightarrow f(0)=0$ , contradiction.
Hence  $f(0)=0$ . $P(x,0)\Rightarrow f(f(x))=f(x)$ If  $f(x)\ne0$  then  $f(x)=x$  by partial injectivity.
Let  $f(a)=0$  and  $f(b)=b$  for some  $a,b\ne0$ : $P(b,a)\Rightarrow f(ab+b)=b\notin\{0,ab+b\}$ , contradiction.
Thus either  $\boxed{f(x)=0}$  or  $\boxed{f(x)=x}$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>The problem is to find all functions  $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  such that:  $$ f(xy + f(x)) = x f(y) + f(x) \quad (*) $$  for all  $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ .

Let  $\mathbf{P}(x, y)$  be the assertion  $f(xy + f(x)) = x f(y) + f(x)$ . $Claim$   $1:$   $f(0)$  is a fixed point of  $f$ .  $$ f(f(0)) = f(0) $$   $Proof:$ Substitute  $x=0$  and  $y=0$  into  $(*)$ :  $$ f(0 \cdot 0 + f(0)) = 0 \cdot f(0) + f(0) $$    $$ f(f(0)) = f(0) $$  This means  $f(0)$  is a fixed point of  $f$ . $\blacksquare$  $Claim$   $2:$   $f(x)$  satisfies  $f(f(x)) = x f(0) + f(x)$ . $Proof:$ Substitute  $y=0$  into  $(*)$ :  $$ f(x \cdot 0 + f(x)) = x f(0) + f(x) $$    $$ f(f(x)) = x f(0) + f(x) \quad (1) $$   $\blacksquare$  $Claim$   $3:$   $f(0) = 0$ . $Proof:$ Let  $c = f(0)$ . From (1), we have:  $$ f(f(x)) - f(x) = c x $$  If  $c \ne 0$ , the right-hand side,  $c x$ , can attain any value in  $\mathbb{R}$ . Thus, the range of  $g(x) = f(f(x)) - f(x)$  is  $\mathbb{R}$ .

Now, substitute  $x=1$  into  $(*)$  (P(1, y)):  $$ f(y + f(1)) = 1 \cdot f(y) + f(1) \quad (2) $$  Let  $a = f(1)$ . Then  $f(y + a) = f(y) + a$ .

Applying (2) repeatedly by induction:  $$ f(y + n a) = f(y) + n a \quad \text{for } n \in \mathbb{N} $$  Substitute  $x=c$  into (1):  $f(f(c)) = c^2 + f(c)$ .
Since  $c = f(0)$ , and  $f(0)$  is in the image of  $f$  (for  $x=1, y=0$ ,  $f(1\cdot 0 + f(1)) = 1 f(0) + f(1)$ ), we can use the property derived from (2) on  $f(c)$ :  $$ f(c + n a) = f(c) + n a $$  Substitute  $f(c + n a)$  into the identity derived from (1):  $$ f(f(n a)) - f(n a) = c (n a) $$  Using  $f(n a) = f(0) + n a = c + n a$ :  $$ f(c + n a) - (c + n a) = c n a $$  Using  $f(c + n a) = f(c) + n a$ :  $$ (f(c) + n a) - (c + n a) = c n a $$    $$ f(c) - c = c n a $$  Since this equation must hold for all  $n \in \mathbb{R}$  (because  $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ ), it requires the coefficient of  $n$  to be zero:  $c a = 0$ .

If  $a = 0$ , then  $f(1)=0$ .  $c$  can still be anything.
If  $a \ne 0$ , then we must have  $c = 0$ .

We must show that the case  $f(1)=0$  and  $f(0)=c \ne 0$  is impossible.
If  $f(1)=0$ , then from  $(*)$ :  $$ f(xy + f(x)) = x f(y) + f(x) $$   $f(f(x)) = c x + f(x)$ . Since  $f(f(1)) = f(0) = c$ ,  $f(1) = 0$ .
Also  $f(f(x))=f(x)$  for all  $x$ . This would imply  $c x + f(x) = f(x)$ , so  $c x = 0$  for all  $x$ , which forces  $c=0$ .
Therefore,  $\mathbf{f(0) = 0}$  must hold. $\blacksquare$  $Claim$   $4:$   $f(x)$  is an idempotent function ( $f(f(x)) = f(x)$ ). $Proof:$ Substitute  $f(0) = 0$  into equation (1) from Claim 2:  $$ f(f(x)) = x \cdot 0 + f(x) $$    $$ f(f(x)) = f(x) \quad (3) $$  This means every value in the image of  $f$  is a fixed point of  $f$ . $\blacksquare$  $Claim$   $5:$  The only solutions are  $f(x) = x$  and  $f(x) = 0$ . $Proof:$ Substitute (3) back into the original equation  $(*)$ :  $$ f(xy + f(x)) = x f(y) + f(x) $$  Consider the image  $I = f(\mathbb{R})$ . Since  $f(z)=z$  for all  $z \in I$ , the term  $f(x)$  is a fixed point.

Let  $y=1$ .  $\mathbf{P}(x, 1)$ :  $$ f(x + f(x)) = x f(1) + f(x) $$  Let  $a=f(1)$ . Since  $a \in I$ ,  $f(a)=a$ .  $$ f(x + f(x)) = a x + f(x) \quad (4) $$  Since  $f(f(x))=f(x)$ , if we let  $x$  be an element in the image,  $x \in I$ , then  $f(x)=x$ .
For  $x \in I$ , (4) becomes:  $$ f(x+x) = a x + x $$    $$ f(2x) = (a+1) x $$  Since  $2x$  is in the image,  $f(2x) = 2x$ .  $$ 2x = (a+1) x $$  Since this must hold for all  $x \in I$ , and  $0 \in I$ , we must have  $2 = a+1$  (assuming  $I$  contains a non-zero element), which implies  $\mathbf{a = 1}$ .
If  $a=1$ , then  $f(1)=1$ .

Now, substitute  $f(1)=1$  into the original equation  $(*)$ : $\mathbf{P}(1, y)$ :  $f(y + f(1)) = 1 f(y) + f(1)$   $$ f(y + 1) = f(y) + 1 $$  This is Cauchy's functional equation on  $\mathbb{Q}$ . Combining  $f(y+1) = f(y)+1$  with  $f(0)=0$  and  $f(f(x))=f(x)$ , the only continuous solution is  $f(x)=x$ . Since we haven't assumed continuity, let's proceed.

From the original equation: $f(xy + f(x)) = x f(y) + f(x)$ If we hypothesize  $\mathbf{f(x) = x}$ :
LHS:  $f(xy + x) = xy + x$ RHS:  $x y + x$ LHS = RHS.  $f(x)=x$  is a solution.

If we hypothesize  $\mathbf{f(x) = 0}$ :
LHS:  $f(xy + 0) = 0$ RHS:  $x \cdot 0 + 0 = 0$ LHS = RHS.  $f(x)=0$  is a solution.

If  $f$  is not the identity or zero function, it must have an image  $I$  where  $|I| \ge 2$ .
If  $a=1$ , then  $f(1)=1$ .
From (4),  $f(x + f(x)) = x + f(x)$ . This means  $x+f(x)$  is in the image, and thus is a fixed point.

Let  $f(x)=y_0$  for some  $y_0 \in I$ . Then: $f(xy + y_0) = x f(y) + y_0$ Let  $x \in I$ , so  $f(x)=x$ . $f(xy + x) = x f(y) + x$ Since  $x \in I$ ,  $f(xy+x)$  must be  $xy+x$ .  $$ xy + x = x f(y) + x $$    $$ xy = x f(y) $$  This must hold for all  $x \in I$ . Since  $I$  contains  $1$  and  $0$ , for  $x=1$ :  $$ y = f(y) $$  Thus,  $f(y)=y$  for all  $y \in \mathbb{R}$ . $\blacksquare$ The only functions satisfying the equation are  $f(x) = x$  and  $f(x) = 0$ .</details>

stem_md: We have a complete graph with  $n$  vertices. We have to color the vertices and the edges in a way such that: no two edges pointing to the same vertice are of the same color; a vertice and an edge pointing him are coloured in a different way. What is the minimum number of colors we need?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>I claim the smallest such amount of colors is  $\boxed{n}$ . We provide a construction first. 

If vertex  $v_i$  is colored  $i$  and  $v_j$  is colored  $j$ , we color the edge  $v_iv_j$  with  $i + j \pmod n$ . Indeed we have that for some arbitrary vertex  $v_0$  that each of the edges are of different color with the remaining  $n - 1$  edges. 

Now we claim the uniqueness of the coloring of every two vertices. Assume that we had the edge  $v_iv_j$  colored as  $i + j \pmod n$ . Assume also that  $v_iv_{j'}$  is colored  $i + j' \pmod n$ . Then we have that if these two edges emanating from  $v_i$  are colored the same, then  $i + j \equiv i + j' \pmod n \implies j = j'$ . Hence we have the minimum colors required is  $\boxed{n}$ .  $\blacksquare$</details>

\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}a_{i}\geq \frac{p^{2}}2 \]
solution_md:
Here's my solution for b).
Let  $A = \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}a_{i}$  and  $B=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}$ . We will prove the inequality for  $B<p$ . By using AM-GM on  $A$  (we take  $p_{i}$   $a_{i}$  times) we get that: $A \geq B \sqrt[B]{(p-1)^{p}+1}\geq B \sqrt[B]{p^{p-1}}.$  If  $B \leq \frac{p-1}{2}$  then  $\sqrt[B]{p^{p-1}}\geq p^{2}$  and we are clearly done. If  $\frac{p-1}{2}< B \leq p-1$  then of course also  $\frac{p}{2}< B$  so  $B \sqrt[B]{p^{p-1}}> \frac{p}{2}p = \frac{p^{2}}{2}$  and in this case the inequality is proved.
Now suppose that  $B \geq p$  and let  $q$  be any prime divisor of  $(p-1)^{p}+1$  which is not  $p$ . Let  $k$  be the order of  $p-1 \mod{q}$ . Since  $(p-1)^{2p}\equiv 1 \mod{q}$ ,  $k|2p$  and  $2|k$  we must have  $k=2$  or  $k=2p$ . The first equality is not possible since we would have  $(p-1) \equiv-1 \mod{q}$  which clearly implies that  $q=p$ . So we have  $k=2p$  and also  $2p|q-1$  so  $q \geq 2p> p$ . Therefore for each  $p_{i}$  we have  $p_{i}\geq p$  so: $A \geq p(a_{1}+a_{2}+...+a_{n}) = pB \geq p^{2}> \frac{p^{2}}{2}$ .

stem_md: Let  $n>1$  be an integer. Let  $p(x)$  be an integer coefficient polynomial with degree  $n$ . Let  $A$  be a set of  $n+1$  consecutive positive integers. Prove that there exist an element  $a \in A$  such that  $p(x)\neq a$  for every integer  $x$ .
solution_md:
Nice. Let  $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_{n+1}\}$  where  $a_{i+1}-a_i=1$  and suppose the contrary that there exists  $x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}$  with  $P(x_i)=a_i$ . By Bezout,  $x_2-x_1\mid P(x_2)-P(x_1)=1$ . As such,  $x_2-x_1=\pm 1$ . Let  $x_2=x_1+1$  (the other case is analogous). By the same reasoning,  $x_3-x_2=\pm 1$ . Further,  $x_3=x_2-1$  is impossible (it'd make  $x_1=x_3$ ). So,  $x_{i+1}-x_i=1$ .

Now, let  $a_1=a$  and  $x_1=x$ . Then,.  $P(x+t) = a+t$  for  $0\le t\le n$ . Consider  $Q(t):=P(x+t)-(a+t)$ , which is of degree  $n$  with  $n+1$  roots, a contradiction.

Prove that for every positive integer  $a$  exists a positive integer  $n$  such that it satisfies the following two conditions:


- The decimal representation of  $a$  is equal to the first part of the (to the left) of the decimal representation of  $n$ .
- If  $m$  is the number obtained from  $n$  by moving from left to right the block containing the digits of  $a$  and cancelling the eventual leading zeros,  $m$  satisfies  $n=am$ .
solution_md: Let  $k$  be the number of digits of  $a$ , and set  $l=s\cdot\varphi(10^ka-1)-k$  where  $s$  is a sufficiently large positive integer (in fact, it need not be that large). Noting that  $b=\frac{a(10^l-a)}{10^ka-1}$  is a positive integer whose number of digits is less than or equal to  $l$ ,  $n=10^la+b$  happens to match our requirement, since  $m=10^kb+a=\frac{n}{a}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ABC$  be a scalene triangle. Let  $X$  and  $Y$  be points respectively on sides  $AB$  and  $AC$ , such that  $BX=CY$ . Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $BC$ ,  $N$  the midpoint of  $XY$ ,  $K$  the intersection of  $XY$  and  $BC$ .
Prove that, as  $X,Y$  vary, the circumcircles of the triangles  $KMN$  have a second common point besides  $M$ .
solution_md:
easy spiral similarity problem
Consider  $P$ , the miquel point of the complete quadrilateral  $BCYX$  (+ $A$  + $K$  of course). Note that this is the center of spiral similarity mapping  $X$  to  $Y$  and  $B$  to  $C$  (or  $X$  to  $B$  and  $Y$  to  $C$ ), so it also maps the midpoint of  $XY$  -  $N$  to the midpoint of  $BC$  -  $M$  and as such  $P$  lies on  $(KMN)$  since  $K$  is the intersection of  $MC$  and  $NY$ .
Now let us prove that  $P$  is fixed.
Since the spiral similarity centered at  $P$  mapping  $X$  to  $Y$  maps  $B$  to  $C$  we have  $\triangle PXB \sim \triangle PYC$  and since  $BX = CY$  the two triangles are congruent, meaning  $PB = PC$  and since  $P$  is on the circumcircle of  $\triangle ABC$ ,  $P$  is a fixed point - the intersection of the perpendicular bisector of  $BC$  with the circumcircle of  $\triangle ABC$ , on the same side of  $BC$  as  $A$ .

Let  $L$  be the midpoint of arc  $\widehat{BAC}$ .
Since  $BL=CL, BX=CY$  and  $\widehat{XBL}=\widehat{YCL}$  we know that triangles  $\Delta BXL$  and  $\Delta CYL$  are congruent, so  $XL=YL$ , and since  $N$  is the midpoint of  $XY$ , we have  $LN\perp NK$ .
We also have  $LM\perp MK$ , so  $L, N, M, K$  are concyclic on the circle of diameter  $KL$ , so  $L$  is the point we're looking for.

stem_md: Prove that for every function  $f:\mathbb{R}^+\mapsto \mathbb{R}^+$  there exist at least two real numbers  $x,y>0$  such that:  $$ f(x+y)<f(x)+yf(f(x)) $$
solution_md:
Suppose the contrary that  $f$  satisfies  $P(x,y)$ , where
\[
P(x,y):\quad f(x+y)\ge f(x) + yf(f(x)),\quad \forall x,y>0.
\]
We prove that no such  $f:\mathbb{R}^+\to\mathbb{R}^+$  exists. Note that  $f$  is clearly increasing and  $P(x,1/f(f(x))$  yields
\[
f\left(x + \frac{1}{f(f(x))}\right)\ge f(x)+1.
\]
We iterate this identity with  $x+1/f(f(x))$  in place of  $x$  to arrive at
\[
f\left(x + \frac{1}{f(f(x))} + \frac{1}{f(f(x+\frac{1}{f(f(x))}))} \right)\ge f(x)+2.
\]
Note that  $f(f(x+1/f(f(x)))\ge f(f(x)+1)$  as  $f$  is increasing. Furthermore,  $P(f(x),1)$  gives  $f(f(x)+1)\ge 2f(f(x))$ . Combining these together with the fact  $f$  is increasing, we get
\[
f\left(x+\frac{1}{f(f(x))}+\frac{1}{2f(f(x))}\right)\ge f(x)+2.
\]
Iterating this identity, we find for every  $n\in\mathbb{N}$ ,
\[
f\left(x+\frac{1}{f(f(x))} \sum_{k=0}^n 2^{-k}\right)\ge f(x)+(n+1).
\]
Fix now an arbitrary  $x_0$  to get
\[
f(x_0 + 2/f(f(x_0))) \ge f(x_0) + n+1.
\]
Since the RHS above is unbounded, we get a contradiction.**Remark.** Very similar to [this Turkish olympiad problem from 1996](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h421476p3455736).

stem_md: When a right triangle is rotated about one leg, the volume of the cone produced is  $800 \pi$   $\text{cm}^3$ .  When the triangle is rotated about the other leg, the volume of the cone produced is  $1920 \pi$   $\text{cm}^3$ .  What is the length (in cm) of the hypotenuse of the triangle?
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the legs of the right triangle be  $x$  and  $y$ . We're trying to find  $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ . Applying the formula for a cone's volume,  $\frac 13 xy^2=800$  and  $\frac 13 x^2y=1920$ . To find  $x$  and  $y$ , we multiply the equations together to obtain  $(\frac 13 xy^2)(\frac 13 x^2y)=\frac 19 x^3y^3=(800)(1920)$ , so that  $xy=240$ . Therefore,  $x=24$  and  $y=10$ , and the hypotenuse is  $\boxed{026}$ .</details>

solution_md: **PP.** A small square is constructed inside a square of area $1$ by dividing each side of the unit square into $n$ equal parts, and then connecting the vertices to the division points closest to the opposite vertices. Find the value of $n$ if the the area of the small square is exactly $\frac {1}{1985}$ .[asy] pair A=(0,1), B=(1,1), C=(1,0), D=origin; draw(A--B--C--D--A--(1,1/6)); draw(C--(0,5/6)^^B--(1/6,0)^^D--(5/6,1)); pair point=( 0.5 , 0.5 ); label(" $A$ ", A, dir(point--A)); label(" $B$ ", B, dir(point--B)); label(" $C$ ", C, dir(point--C)); label(" $D$ ", D, dir(point--D)); label(" $1/n$ ", (11/12,1), N, fontsize(9));[/asy]**Proof.** Let $M\in (AD)$ and $N\in (AB)$ so that $AM=NB=\frac 1n\ ,\ m\left(\widehat{ADN}\right)=\phi $ and the sidelength $l$ of the small square. Observe that $\boxed{l=AM\cdot \cos\phi}\ (*)\ , \tan\phi =\frac {AN}{AD}=\frac {n-1}{n}$ . Therefore, $\cos\phi =\frac {1}{\sqrt{1+\tan^2\phi}}=$ $\frac {n}{\sqrt{n^2+(n-1)^2}}\stackrel{(*)}{\implies}$ $\frac {1}{\sqrt {1985}}=\frac 1n\cdot \frac {n}{\sqrt{n^2+(n-1)^2}}\iff$ $2n^2-2n+1=1985\iff$ $n(n-1)=992=32\cdot 31\iff$ $\boxed{n=32}$ .

The sum of the following seven numbers is exactly 19: 
\[a_1=2.56,\qquad a_2=2.61,\qquad a_3=2.65,\qquad a_4=2.71,\]
\[a_5=2.79,\qquad a_6=2.82,\qquad a_7=2.86.\]

solution_md: <details><summary>Answer</summary>To sum to  $19$ , we need two 2's and five 3's. Obviously, rounding any number greater than one of the first two to  $2$  will give a greater error than rounding the first two to  $2$ , and the other five will round to  $3$ . The largest error is therefore  $|A_2-a_2|=0.61=M$ , so  $100M=\boxed{061}$ .</details>

stem_md: Assume that  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ , and  $d$  are positive integers such that  $a^5 = b^4$ ,  $c^3 = d^2$ , and  $c - a = 19$ .  Determine  $d - b$ .
solution_md:
Solution$a^5 = b^4 \implies a = e^4, b = e^5$ for some integer $e$ . Similarly, $c^3 = d^2 \implies c = f^2, d = f^3$ for some integer $f$ . We are given $f^2 - e^4 = 19$ and asked to find $f^3 - e^5$ . $f^2 - e^4 = (f + e^2)(f - e^2) = 19$ . Clearly, $f - e^2 = 1, f + e^2 = 19, e = 3, f = 10$ . Then $f^3 - e^5 = 1000 - 729 = \boxed{271}$ .

stem_md: In a circle, parallel chords of lengths 2, 3, and 4 determine central angles of  $\alpha$ ,  $\beta$ , and  $\alpha + \beta$  radians, respectively, where  $\alpha + \beta < \pi$ .  If  $\cos \alpha$ , which is a positive rational number, is expressed as a fraction in lowest terms, what is the sum of its numerator and denominator?
solution_md: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>If we let  $\frac{\alpha}{2} = x$  and  $\frac{\beta}{2} = y$  we have  $\sin x = \frac 1r$ ,  $\sin y = \frac 3{2r}$  and  $\sin(x+y) = \frac 2r$ . $\sin x \cos y + \sin y \cos x = \frac 2r$  $\frac 1r \cdot \frac{\sqrt{r^2 - \frac 94}}{r} + \frac 3{2r} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{r^2 - 1}}{r} = \frac 2r$  $r=\frac 8{\sqrt{15}}$  $\cos \alpha = 2 \cos^2 x - 1$  $\cos x = \frac{\sqrt{r^2-1}}{r}$  so we have  $\cos a = 1 - \frac 2{r^2} = 1- \frac{15}{32} = \frac{17}{32}$ The answer is  $17+32=49$</details>

stem_md:
How many of the first 1000 positive integers can be expressed in the form
\[ \lfloor 2x \rfloor + \lfloor 4x \rfloor + \lfloor 6x \rfloor + \lfloor 8x \rfloor, \]
where  $x$  is a real number, and  $\lfloor z \rfloor$  denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to  $z$ ?
solution_md:
SOLUTION 1
We can experiment with all numbers less than or equal to one in the form  $\frac{m}{24}$ :  $\frac{1}{24}, \frac{2}{24} \to 0$ ,  $\frac{3}{24} \to 1, \frac{4}{24}$ ,  $\frac{5}{24} \to 2$ ,  $\frac{6}{24}$ ,  $\frac{7}{24} \to 4$ ,  $\frac{8}{24} \to 5$ ,  $\frac{9}{24}$ ,  $\frac{10}{24}$ ,  $\frac{11}{24} \to 6$ ,  $\frac{12}{24}$ ,  $\frac{13}{24}$ ,  $\frac{14}{24} \to 10$ ,  $\frac{15}{24} \to 11$ ,  $\frac{16}{24},\frac{17}{24} \to 12$ , $\frac{18}{24}, \frac{19}{24} \to 14$ ,  $\frac{20}{24}\to 15$ ,  $\frac{21}{24}, \frac{22}{24}, \frac{23}{24} \to16$ ,  $\frac{24}{24} \to 20$ . We can easily that that  $12$  of  $20$  numbers can be achieved. Extending this, of the first  $1000$  numbers, there are  $\frac{12}{20} \cdot 1000 = \boxed{600}$  possible values.

SOLUTION 2
Imagine that we increase  $x$  from  $0$  to  $1$  as the values goes from  $0$  to  $2+4+6+8=20$ . We seek to find how many integers between  $1$  and  $20$  we skipped. We skip whenever  $2x$ ,  $4x$ ,  $6x$ , and  $8x$  become integers at simultaneously.

When  $x=1/2$  and  $x=1$ , all four values become integers at the same time, so skip three integers, and when  $x=1/4$  and  $x=3/4$ , the values  $4x$  and  $8x$  become integers at the same time, so we skip one integer for both.

In total we skip  $3+3+1+1=8$  of the first  $20$  integers. Extending this, of the first  $1000$  numbers, there are  $\frac{12}{20} \cdot 1000 = \boxed{600}$  values.

stem_md: In a tournament each player played exactly one game against each of the other players.  In each game the winner was awarded 1 point, the loser got 0 points, and each of the two players earned 1/2 point if the game was a tie.  After the completion of the tournament, it was found that exactly half of the points earned by each player were earned against the ten players with the least number of points.  (In particular, each of the ten lowest scoring players earned half of her/his points against the other nine of the ten).  What was the total number of players in the tournament?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let there be  $N$  players. Then, note that each of the  $10$  lowest-scoring players must earn half of their points against each other and each of the  $N-10$  highest-scoring players must earn half of their points against each other. Therefore, the  $10$  lowest-scoring players earn  $\tbinom{10}{2}$  total points against each other and  $\tbinom{10}{2}$  total points against the  $N-10$  highest-scoring players and the  $N-10$  highest-scoring players earn  $\tbinom{N-10}{2}$  total points against each other and  $\tbinom{N-10}{2}$  total points against the lowest-scoring players. Therefore, since the total number of points earned is clearly  $\tbinom{N}{2},$  we get
\begin{align*}
    2\cdot \binom{10}{2} + 2 \cdot \binom{N-10}{2} = \binom{N}{2} &\implies 90 + (N-10)(N-11) = \frac{N(N-1)}{2} 
    &\implies 180+2N^2-42N+220=N^2-N 
    &\implies N^2- 41N+400=0 
    &\implies (N-25)(N-16)=0 
    &\implies N=25 \text{ or } N=16.
\end{align*}
However, note that if  $N=16,$  then the  $N-10$  players from before wouldn't actually be the highest scoring players. Therefore, the answer is  $N=\boxed{25}.$   $\square$</details>

Note that the condition tells us that half of the points of the total,  $\frac{1}{2}\cdot \binom{n}{2}$  is from the games between the  $10$  and the  $n-10$  players, so  $$ \frac{1}{2}\cdot \binom{n}{2} = (n-10)10 $$    $$ n = 16 \text{ or } n = 25 $$  If  $n$  is  $16$ , it's easy to calculate that the average of the  $6$  biggest players is  $\frac{30}{6}=5$ , while the average of the  $10$  smallest is  $\frac{120-30}{10} = 9$ , a contradiction. The key is to <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>use a global approach and consider the sum of points in certain cases.</details>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let there be  $n$  players. Since  $\binom{n}{2}$  games are played, there are  $\binom{n}{2}$  points total. 
Within the  $10$  worst players,  $\binom{10}{2}$  games are played, so the sum of their points is  $2\binom{10}{2}$ . 
Within the other  $n-10$  players, each player scored half of their points with the other  $n-11$ . The sum of the points in this group of players is thus  $2\binom{n-10}{2}$ .
Therefore, we have  $$ 2\binom{10}{2}+2\binom{n-10}{2}=\binom{n}{2} $$    $$ 180+2(n-10)(n-11)=n(n-1) $$    $$ 2n^2-42n+400=n^2-n $$    $$ n^2-41n+400=0 $$    $$ n=16,25 $$  However,  $16$  is not possible because it would cause the mean score of the  $10$  worst to be  $9$ , and the mean of the  $6$  best to be  $5$ . Hence,  $\boxed{25}$  is the answer.</details>

We say that a team is a loser if it is in the bottom 10 teams, and we say that a team is a winner otherwise. Let  $n$  be the number of winners.

We break this up into three seperate tournaments, which we denote as  $T_1,T_2,T_3.$  In  $T_1$ , each possible pairing of two losers is played. In  $T_2$ , each possible pairing of a loser and a winner is played, and in  $T_3$ , each possible pairing of two winners is played. The total number of games (and thus total points scored) is 45 in  $T_1$ ,  $10n$  in  $T_2$ , and  $n\choose 2$  in  $T_3.$ Note that by summing the condition over all loser teams, we see that the number of points scored by losers against other losers (which is 45 from  $T_1$ ) is the same as the number of points scored by losers against winners, so the losers score a total of 45 points in  $T_2$ . Similarly, the winners score a total of  $n\choose 2$  points in  $T_2$  against losers since they also scored that many points against other winners. This gives us the identity   $$ 45+{n\choose 2}=10n. $$   Expanding out the quadratic, the solutions are  $n=6$  and  $n=15$ . However,  $n=6$  is not possible since that would imply that each loser score more points on average than each winner on average, which is not possible since the losers are the bottom 10, so  $n=15$  and our answer is  $\textbf{25}.$

Let there be $n+10$ players in the tournament. Split these players into two groups, one group of the bottom $10$ players, called team $B$ , and another group of the remaining top $n$ players, called team $A$ . Notice that we always have a constant $\binom{n+10}{2}$ points circulating in the system. Between $A$ group, there are $\binom{n}{2}$ points, and between $B$ group, there are $\binom{10}{2}$ points. Since each group earned half of its points from people in their group and the other half from the other group, we also have that $2\left[\binom{n}{2}+\binom{10}{2}\right]=\binom{n+10}{2}$ . Expanding the quadratic equation and solving, we have that either $n=15$ or $n=6$ , but $n=6$ yields a contradiction to the fact that the $6$ players must be the top $6$ players*, meaning that we must have $25$ players in this tournament, and we are done. *If we have $16$ total players, we have that the group of top $k$ players score a total of $30$ points while the bottom $10$ players score a total of $90$ points. However, by average properties, we have that out of the top $6$ players, the maximum of the minimum of points scored out of the top $6$ players is $\frac{30}{6}=5$ , meaning that the $10$ other players could have scored a maximum of $10*5=50$ points, a contradiction. Therefore $k=6$ is extraneous, giving us that $k=15$ , for a total of $25$ players in the tournament.

This took me 45 minutes, to find the elegant way. We can let there be  $x+10$ , players in the tournament. We then make  $2$  teams, one with the bottom  $10$  which is team  $A$ , and the other team with the remaining players, called team  $B$ , there is always  $\binom{x+10}{2}$ , points. We have  $2\binom{x}{2}+2\binom{10}{2}=\binom{x+10}{2}$ , solving we get  $x=6$ , or  $x=15$ , if  $x=6$ , leads to a contradiction. So  $x+10=\boxed{25}.$

We can see that the ten lowest players score  $\binom{10}{2} = 45$  points among themselves. This means that they score  $45$  points against all of the other players. Let there be  $x$  players in the tournament discluding the  $10$  lowest scoring players. This means that those players score  $10x-45$  point against the  $10$  lowest scoring players. Also they score  $\binom{x}{2}$  points among themselves. We can easily see that   $$ \binom{x}{2} = 10x - 45 $$  We can easily extract with quadratic formula that  $x = 15 \Rightarrow \boxed{025}$ .  $\blacksquare$

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Say that there are  $x$  teams not in the bottom  $10$ . The total number of points scored in games with the bottom  $10$  is  $45+10n$ We obtain from the problem statement  $45 + \binom{n}{2}=10n$ So  $n=15$ . So there are  $25$  players.</details>

Let there be  $k$  other people, not in the bottom ten. In the bottom ten, there are  $45$  points in total, so the bottom ten must have scored  $45$  points against the  $k$  other people. This means the  $k$  other people scored  $10k-45$  which is equal to the amount of points they scored among themselves, or  $\binom{k}{2}$ . Thus,

\[\binom{k}{2}=10k-45\]
\[\implies k=6,15\]

Then, note that  $k=6$  does not work, so our answer is  $10+15=\boxed{025}$ .

Call the ten lowest scoring players "bad players" and call everyone else "good players".

Note that the bad players collectively got half of their points from the good players, and the good players collectively got half of their points from the bad players. If the bad players collectively scored  $x$  points and the good players collectively scored  $y$  points and there are  $n$  good players, we have
\[\frac x2+\frac y2=10n\]
\[x+y=\binom{10+n}{2}\]
therefore
\[40n=(n+10)(n+9)=n^2+19n+90\Longrightarrow n^2-21n+90=0.\]
So  $n=6$  or  $n=15$ . From here it is intuitive that  $n=6$  doesn't make sense(since then the players all did better against the good players than the bad players), so the answer is  $10+15=\boxed{25}$ .

Let  $a$  be the sum of points of the top  $n-10$  players, and let  $b$  be the sum of the points of the last  $10$  players. We have  $\frac{a}{2}+\frac{b}{2} = 10(n-1)-b$ . We also have  $10(n-1)-b = \binom{10}{2}+\frac{a}{2}$ . This gives  $b=90$ , so we have \[a+b=\binom{n}{2}=10(n-1)-90,\] giving  $n^2-41n+400=0$ . Hence,  $n=16,25$  and  $25$  is the only one that works because otherwise the average of the lowest ten players would be  $\frac{90}{10}=9$  while the average of the higher  $6$  would be  $\frac{\binom{16}{2}-90}{6}=5$ , giving a contradiction.

Suppose there are  $n + 10$  players, and  $p$  points are earned altogether against the ten lowest scoring players. We will double-count  $p$ . 

The conditions of the problem tell us that  $p = \frac{1}{2} \binom{n + 10}{2}$ . Now on the other hand, we know that  $45$  points are earned by the bottom  $10$  players competing amongst themselves. The condition of the problem summed along the top  $n$  players tells us that the number of points earned by the  $n$  players amongst themselves equals the number of points earned against the bottom  $10$  players, which equates to  $\binom{n}{2}$ . So we have   $$ p = \frac{1}{2} \binom{n + 10}{2} = 45 + \binom{n}{2} \implies (n - 15)(n - 6) = 0. $$  Note that  $n = 6$  is extraneous so we have  $15 + 10 = \boxed{25}$  people who participated in the tournament.

The answer is $\fbox{25}$ . Let $B$ denote the set containing the worst ten players, and $G$ the set containing all other players. Let $P = B \cap G$ be the set of all players. We'll make use of the following notation: for two subsets of players $X$ and $Y$ , let $S_{X \rightarrow Y}$ denote the total number of points won by players in $X$ over players in $Y$ . **Claim:** $n \in \{16, 25\}$ . *Proof.* Our goal is to double count $S_{P \rightarrow B}$ . By summing over all players, this is half the total number of points won, which gives \[S_{P \rightarrow B} = \frac12 \binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n - 1)}{4}\] since each game is worth $1$ point. On the other hand, we have $S_{P \rightarrow B} = S_{G \rightarrow B} + S_{B \rightarrow B}$ , so it suffices to compute $S_{G \rightarrow B}$ and $S_{B \rightarrow B}$ . The latter is just $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ , since $S_{B \rightarrow B}$ counts the total number of points in the games within $B$ . We also have \[S_{G \rightarrow B} = \frac12 S_{G \rightarrow P} = \frac12(S_{G \rightarrow B} + S_{G \rightarrow G}) = \frac12\left(S_{G \rightarrow B} + \binom{n - 10}{2}\right),\] so $S_{G \rightarrow B} = \binom{n - 10}{2} = \frac{(n - 10)(n - 11)}{2}$ . Putting this together, we have \[\frac{n(n - 1)}{4} = \frac{(n - 10)(n - 11)}{2} + 45,\] which reduces to $(n - 16)(n - 25) = 0$ as desired. $\square$ **Claim:** $n \neq 16$ . *Proof.* Suppose $n = 16$ is possible. Since each player in $G$ scores at least as many points as each player in $B$ , we have \[\frac{S_{G \rightarrow P}}{6} \geq \frac{S_{B \rightarrow P}}{10}.\] But $S_{G \rightarrow P} = 2S_{G \rightarrow B} = (16 - 10)(16 - 11) = 30$ and $S_{B \rightarrow P} = \binom{16}{2} - 30 = 90$ , which is absurd. $\square$ This implies that $n = 25$ , as predicted. $\square$

Let there be  $n$  people. It's easy to see that the bottom ten people in total scored  $\binom{10}{2} \cdot 2 = 90$  points. Then  $\frac{\binom{n}{2}-90}{2}$  points are won by the top  $n-10$  people *against* the bottom  $10$  people. We can also count this as  $10(n-10)-45$  where the  $45$  comes from the points out of the  $10(n-10)$  being won by the bottom  $10$ . Equating:   $$ \frac{\binom{n}{2}-90}{2} = 10(n-10)-45 \implies n = 16, 25 $$   But  $n=16$  doesn't make any sense so we have  $n = \boxed{25}$

Let  $n$  be the total number of players. A total of 45 points are made between the bottom 10 and the other  $n - 10$  people. There are also  $\binom{n - 10}2$  points containing only the top  $n - 10$ . Thus,  $n^2 - 21n + 110= 20n - 290\implies n^2 - 41n + 255 = 0 \implies n = 16, 25.$  However, if  $n = 16,$  the 10 people aren't the weakest. Thus,  $n = \boxed{20}.$

stem_md: Let  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$ , and  $D$  be the vertices of a regular tetrahedron, each of whose edges measures 1 meter.  A bug, starting from vertex  $A$ , observes the following rule: at each vertex it chooses one of the three edges meeting at that vertex, each edge being equally likely to be chosen, and crawls along that edge to the vertex at its opposite end.  Let  $p = n/729$  be the probability that the bug is at vertex  $A$  when it has crawled exactly 7 meters.  Find the value of  $n$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Note that this problem is basically equivalent to the following: How many distinct sequences of  $8$  integers  $a_1, a_2, a_3, ..., a_8$  are there such that  $a_1 = a_8 = 1,$   $a_i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$  for all  $2 \leq i\leq 8,$  and  $a_i \neq a_{i+1}$  for all  $1 \leq i \leq 7$ ?

Now consider the  $8$  integers modulo  $4.$  Let  $b_1, b_2, b_3, ..., b_7$  be a new sequence of integers such that  $b_i = a_{i+1} - a_i \mod 4$  for all  $1 \leq i \leq 7.$ Note that the condition is equivalent to that  $b_i \in \{1, 2, 3\}$  for all  $1 \leq i \leq 7,$  and since  $a_1 \mod 4 = a_8 \mod 4,$   $b_1 + b_2 + ... + b_7$  must be a multiple of  $4.$ Thus, our desired number of paths is equivalent to the number of ordered septuples of positive integers  $(b_1, b_2, ..., b_7)$  such that  $b_i \in \{1, 2, 3\}$  for all  $1 \leq i \leq 7$  and  $b_1 + b_2 + ... + b_7$  is congruent to  $0 \mod 4.$ We will now proceed with casework on the number of  $2$ s in the septuple.

One  $2$ :  $\dbinom{7}{1} = 7$  ways to arrange the  $2$ , and  $\dbinom{6}{0} + \dbinom{6}{2} + \dbinom{6}{4} + \dbinom{6}{6} = 2^5$  valid ways (the proof of this combinatorial identity is left as an exercise to the reader) to arrange the  $1$ s and  $3$ s

Three  $2$ s:  $\dbinom{7}{3} = 35$  ways to arrange the  $2$ s, and  $\dbinom{4}{1} + \dbinom{4}{3} = 2^3$  valid ways to arrange the  $1$ s and  $3$ s

Five  $2$ s:  $\dbinom{7}{5} = 21$  ways to arrange the  $2$ s, and  $\dbinom{2}{0} + \dbinom{2}{2} = 2$  valid ways to arrange the  $1$ s and  $3$ s

Adding up our cases, we obtain  $7 \cdot 32 + 35 \cdot 8 + 21 \cdot 2 = 546$  valid sequences. Dividing by the total number of paths without restrictions,  $3^7 = 2187,$  our desired probability is  $\frac{546}{2187} = \frac{182}{729},$  giving an answer of  $\boxed{182}.$</details>

The tetrahedron is basically the graph K4, and has an adjacency matrix with 0's along its main diagonal and 1's everywhere else.  Raise this matrix to the 7th power to find the number of paths of length 7 from any given vertex to another.  This matrix has 546's along its main diagonal and 547's everywhere else. **Proposition:** The eigenvalues of the matrix you wrote down are $ 1, \minus{} \frac {1}{3}, \minus{} \frac {1}{3}, \minus{} \frac {1}{3}$ . **Lemma:** Let $ P$ be a stochastic matrix. The probability that after $ n$ steps you return to the same state as the state in which you started is the sum of the $ n^{th}$ powers of the eigenvalues of $ P$ .
So...Since the probability of returning to the same vertex is the same for each vertex, divide by $ 4$ : the final answer is $ \frac {1}{4} \left( 1 \minus{} \frac {3}{3^7} \right) \equal{} \frac {3^6 \minus{} 1}{4 \cdot 3^6} \equal{} \frac {182}{729}$ . :)

In general you'd either need to work directly with the matrix or compute eigenvectors.  Closed walks are unique because they depend on the eigenvalues only.  There is a theorem which tells you how to do this without computing eigenvectors, but it is somewhat indirect.
**Theorem (4.7.2 in Stanley, *Enumerative Combinatorics*):**  For an adjacency matrix  $ A$ , let  $ a_{ij}(n)$  denote the number of walks of length  $ n$  from vertex  $ i$  to vertex  $ j$  and let  $ A[ij]$  denote the matrix obtained from  $ A$  by deleting the  $ i^{th}$  column and  $ j^{th}$  row.  Then
 $ \sum_{n \ge 0} a_{ij}(n) \lambda^n \equal{} \frac {( \minus{} 1)^{i \plus{} j} \det(I \minus{} \lambda A[ij]) }{\det(I \minus{} \lambda A) }$ .

solution_md:
Prove that a circle centered at point $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$ in the cartesian plane passes through at most one point with integer coordinates. I tried to prove that any circle with center at $(0,0)$ has at most one point with coordinates $(a-\sqrt{2},b-\sqrt{3})$ ; $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$ . So that when we translate the center to $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$ we have what we wanted to show.
I think the approach below is probably a simpler one, though there may be other equally simple ways of solving the problem. Let us assume, for the sake of contradiction, there is a circle with center $O(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$ such that it passes through two points with integer coordinates. Let these two points be $A(a,b)$ and $B(c,d),$ where $a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Note that the line $AB$ is a chord of the circle. Let the midpoint of $AB$ be $C,$ where $C\equiv (\frac{a+c}{2}, \frac{b+d}{2}).$ Let $L$ denote the line passing through $C$ and perpendicular to $AB.$ Now, slope of line $AB$ equals $\frac{b-d}{a-c}\Rightarrow$ Slope of the line $L$ equals $\frac{a-c}{d-b}.$ So, the equation of line $L$ is given by $y-\frac{b+d}{2}={(\frac{a-c}{d-b})}(x-\frac{a+c}{2})$ Since $L$ , passes through the point $O$ , we must have $\sqrt{3}-m = n(\sqrt{2}-p),$ where $m=\frac{b+d}{2}, n=\frac{a-c}{d-b}$ and $p=\frac{a+c}{2}.$ Note that $m,n$ and $p$ are all rational. So, we get $\sqrt{3}-n\sqrt{2}= m-np$ $\Rightarrow 3+2n^{2}-2n\sqrt{6}={(m-np)}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{6}$ is rational, which is clearly a contradiction. Hence no such circle exists.

stem_md:
Let  $a_1,a_2,...$  and  $b_1,b_2,..$ . be two arbitrary infinite sequences of natural numbers. 
Prove that there exist different indices  $r$  and  $s$  such that  $a_r \ge a_s$  and  $b_r \ge b_s$ .
solution_md:
Call a number BIG in the sequence if it is larger than all the numbers before it in the sequence.
Call a number SMALL if it is lesser than all the numbers before it., If either sequence is bounded above, then the problem is trivial, so assume that neither of the sequences are bounded above.
<details><summary>Here's the proof of bounded sequences anyways</summary>If some sequence, WLOG  $a_n$  is bounded, then some number  $p$  appears infinitely many times, say at indices  $a_{i_1}, a_{i_2}, \cdots$ , then the counterparts  $b_{i_1}, b_{i_2}, \cdots $  form a strictly decreasing sequence, but naturals are bounded below, contradiction.</details>

So, for the first Big number in the first sequence, say  $a_r$ , then  $a_r > a_1, a_2 \cdots a_{r-1}$ . If  $b_r  \geq b_i$  for some  $i <r$ , then we are done, so assume  $b_r < b_1, b_2 \cdots b_{r-1}$ . So  $b_r$  is small whenever  $a_r$  is big. But since  $a_n$  is not bounded, there will be infinitely many big numbers. However, there cannot be infinitely small numbers because Natural numbers are bounded below by  $1$ . Hence, we will have  $b_r \geq b_s$  and  $a_r \geq a_s$  simultaneously.

stem_md: Players  $A$  and  $B$  play the following game:  $A$  tosses a coin  $n$  times, and  $B$  does  $n+1$  times. The player who obtains more ”heads” wins; or in the case of equal balances,  $A$  is assigned victory. Find the values of  $n$  for which this game is fair (i.e. both players have equal chances for victory).
solution_md:
We claim this game is fair for all  $n \ge 0$ .

The result is trivial for  $n = 0$ . If  $n \ge 1$ , then the following argument suffices: 


- Consider the first  $n$  flips player  $B$  makes.
- If player  $A$  has obtained more heads at this point, then they're guaranteed to win.
- If player  $B$  has already obtained more heads at this point, then they're guaranteed to win.
- By symmetry, the two aforementioned cases have an equal chance of occurring.
- If player  $A$  and player  $B$  have both obtained an equal number of heads at this point, then: player  $A$  wins if player  $B$  flips tails on their  $n+1$ th flip, and player  $B$  wins if they flip heads on their  $n+1$ th flip.
- But both of these events have an equal chance of happening, which means we've shown this game is fair for all  $n \ge 1$ .

Combining these  $2$  results yields our original claim, so we're done.  $\blacksquare$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Italy Contests/ITAMO/1988 ITAMO/1998788.json

candidates: B wins if A obtains  $k$  heads and  $B$  obtains  $k+1,k+2,...$  or  $n+1$  heads  $$ \frac12=\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{{n\choose k}}{2^n}\cdot\frac{\sum_{i=k+1}^{n+1}{n+1\choose i}}{2^{n+1}} $$

Let p be the probability that A will get at least as many heads as B if A throws a coin n times and B throws a coin n times.
The first scenario is when A wins if B's first flip is the tail and A gets at least as many heads as B in the next n tosses. The probability that A will win is p.
The second scenario is when B's first flip is the head, A wins over the next n tosses, and A becomes larger than B has the same number of heads. This means that the probability of A winning in this scenario is 1-p.
Since both scenarios can occur equally, the probability of A winning is 1/2*p+1/2*(1-p)=1/2. Thus, the game is always fair for any integer n.

stem_md: The edge lengths of the base of a tetrahedron are  $a,b,c$ , and the lateral edge lengths are  $x,y,z$ . If  $d$  is the distance from the top vertex to the centroid of the base, prove that  $x+y+z \le  a+b+c+3d$ .
solution_md:
Label the given tetrahedron by  $T_0$  and define  $T_{n+1}$  as the tetrahedron with the same vertex as  $T_n$  and with the base being the medial triangle of  $T_n$ .
Let  $x_1, y_1, k_1$  be the medians in the respective lateral faces of  $a, b, c$  (which are also the lateral edges of  $T_1$ ). Note that  $y+z< a+2x_1$ . In fact  $$ y+z-a< \sqrt{2y^2+2z^2-a^2} \iff 0<(y+z)^2+2a(y+z-a). $$  Summing up it with the analogous inequalities  $z+x<b+2y_1$  and  $x+y<c+2z_1$  we get  $$ x+y+z<\frac{a+b+c}{2}+x_1+y_1+z_1. $$  Repeating this procedure  $n$  times we get  $$ x+y+z<\frac{(2^n-1)(a+b+c)}{2^n}+x_n+y_n+z_n $$  where  $x_n, y_n, z_n$  are the lateral edge lengths of  $T_n$ . Taking  $n$  to infinity gives  $$ x+y+z\le a+b+c+3d $$  Q.E.D.
